Skills and tools in this layer
a2a6948703ae: One testable idea about a method is a folder in the work repository. The H-XXX code is given once and stays after testing: it shows the grounds, the history, and the conclusion.
83a2aeacdefa: One sentence you can read aloud: what we claim and under which conditions. Code checks this, not the writer's good faith.
20d343742bc1: What exactly would refute the idea. Without a falsification criterion it is not a claim.
85950cf57c46: Runs and series in runs/ and series/, derivations in theory/, figures in figures/: next to it, in the same folder.
ce406045620b: draft → testing → supported, refuted, or inconclusive, and it changes only by its own criterion.
a4449f57aa2c: The work and theme are visible from the path, the history from git: who wrote it, when, and with which merge request.
6e1e005187f9: A claim tested by measurement. Code writes the runs, and series gather them to answer one question.
a116204fba86: By series of runs: every number has an address where it can be seen.
06d3beac0dde: A claim tested by mathematical derivation. The assumptions and the proof live in a derivation file next to the claim.
106a9e6fd323: By a derivation with explicit assumptions and a “Proof” section.
542fdeadfad8: An ideal claim holds both theory and experiments about one technique: a theorem and runs about the same thing are one folder, not two.
988ab6616e76: So that a work has a handful of claims rather than a hundred, and each one can be read in full.
f8c5fe07c0b1: An idea from an external work: what its authors claim and where to find it. A paper analysis is a page in the theme literature repository, one per paper.
4446ef08828b: A result, theorem, method, or definition.
8deef35826e7: A section, table, formula, or theorem of the paper; the citation key and BibTeX are in the page header.
bb31b7896a94: Our work links to the analysis: background, baseline, supports, or contradicts. A link alone does not complete our own check.
d0e1ecb54c34: You can compare the reported result with your own run and find the original table.
6e474678af2c: A theorem, lemma, bound, or derivation from the paper. The statement keeps the assumptions, and the pointer leads to where the proof is.
4bc2a208806a: What the authors propose to do: an algorithm, a training technique, or a procedure. The method description is kept apart from the claim about its effectiveness.
ffb5e69ed179: How the authors define a concept or a quantity. Helps compare works in which the same word means different things.
e66869bbae48: The state changes on the same claim and only by its own criterion. A finished run does not change the state by itself: a person or an agent formulates the conclusion, and a person merges it.
156926f1bff2: draft → testing with the first series.
355972f637d0: Only a fully examined claim has a “Conclusion” section: under draft and testing there is none, otherwise it promises what is not there yet.
7d5ec07ee3b1: Every change is a merge commit: you can see who changed the state, when, and on what grounds.
6530d33b4df6: The runs finished, but the results differ between repeats. Claim: inconclusive, and the series says why.
27a32a6965c2: The page of a single launch. Code writes it: the lab_run.py recorder knows the hyperparameters, numbers, commit, and hardware, and copying them by hand is forbidden.
2ab2404c2d6f: Command, configuration, environment, commit, hardware, and metrics, as the recorder wrote them.
ef01018b0ed8: Exactly one thing: what is seen in these numbers.
9b3ffd2528e8: Comparing A and B on one model and dataset with the same budget: three seeds, each with its own page.
e41f13e0774e: A set of runs that answers one question, and a verdict on it. A series enters the claim as a paragraph.
dab74997e9fa: A table of runs and numbers; every number has an address where it can be seen.
b63302f3e631: Verdict and limits: “not established” is also a valid verdict.
78d5fff9b9a8: Incomparable runs are not pulled into a series; a run outside a series says so on its own page.
d96e53162c2a: The mathematical basis of a claim: statement, assumptions, and a “Proof” section. One file per storyline, not per lemma.
11bfacffec3b: Reads from scratch and contains no numbers from a specific run.
af989efab543: A derivation lives only if it says where it works in the claim.
2a23183214f1: One repository per work. The front page answers in one order: what we claim, what it has been tested with, what is open.
2c5fe5e2fd83: claims/ is knowledge; paper/ and code/ are the manuscript and code as nested repositories; socials/ and calls/ are posters and calls.
2fb48840d308: The “Leads” and “Team” lines in the README: the bot uses them to call people to decide access requests, and merge requests are assigned to the lead.
45f459fc68cf: Every theme has its own repository of analyses: one page per paper, named after the paper, with the citation key in the header. The literature README is assembled from the pages themselves.
be8ccca7eae1: From a statement in our work you can go back to the full analysis. One paper can be needed by many works.
6c211b062f4b: Every record in a work comes in as a merge request: branch, commit, git push, and the merge request opens by itself. The gates count numbers and judge prose, a person merges.
c4226d85d21c: Three things: what changed, what it rests on, what is still open.
f5de4ceae379: The lead of the work. An agent merges only on a named person's word and writes in the merge request on whose word.
abbece22311e: The merge is the record. A branch, a draft, and a note are not records.
7b420f6184b3: Branch claim/H-XXX-001: a new series of runs and a paragraph in the claim. The gates are green, the lead merged.
fe66b02b6fbd: A chronicle of how the lab works: a new rule, a new place, a disabled tool, with a date, newest on top.
d4d4de129731: What someone will look for in a month and be upset not to find.
80abd71f8bb5: A plain push to main after git pull --rebase: this is a service repository.
81bf1601f956: “The lab is installed as one tree ~/brainlab: lab sync gathers everything you can see”.
60a11ae98c01: The definition of an internal name: a method, run, metric, or protocol. A name is defined before its first use.
7538aac3350f: A person or an agent will decode an old record without its author.
7bce8ef63b3e: What matters about the hardware: what changed, what does not work, where access changed. Ephemeral state such as a free GPU is not here; it is checked with a command.
1d155f856930: A run does not start or an address does not respond: look here first.
4e1e0b2eb89a: Where a record came from and how it changed: the commit, its author and time, the merge request with its discussion and the gates' verdict.

The setup does not know that scientific claims are inside. Product, analytics, market research, or engineering: wherever decisions rest on verifiable grounds, the same order works.

Four rules

  1. A work is a repository

    Each has its own place, its own people, and its own history. Rights are inherited down the tree, as with GitLab groups.

  2. An idea is a folder

    A claim and everything that grounds it sit next to each other as files. No form for form's sake: the page is read by eye.

  3. A record is a merge

    Agents and people propose, the gates check numbers and prose, a person accepts. Junk does not get into the base.

  4. Everyone has the tree

    The whole base sits locally as one tree and opens in Obsidian. Work is plain git: edit, branch, push.

One way to save

  1. An edit on its own branch

    The agent edits files on a separate branch and pushes them with one command: GitLab opens the proposal itself and assigns the work lead.

  2. Code runs the checks

    Every number is checked against the runs: a number found in no run blocks the merge. Record codes, links and file deletions are checked the same way. A judge model reads the text separately, looking for filler and for conclusions that do not follow from what is written.

    The verdict arrives 28 seconds after a proposal is opened, and the text judge costs about $0.3 a month for the whole flow.

Open the access bot ↗
